blocks.text: The account displays detailed knowledge of ancient Mediterranean sailing, tracing changing winds, sheltered routes, efforts to reinforce and lighten the ship, depth soundings, anchoring, and the final attempt to reach shore. Even with this level of detail, the precise location of the wreck and the extent to which the narrative depends on eyewitness experience remain disputed.

Acts survives in several early papyri and major Greek codices. P45, P53, P74, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae preserve different portions and sometimes different textual profiles, so the wording of Acts is studied by comparing multiple witnesses rather than relying on a single surviving manuscript.

Acts 27 belongs to several sections of the book that use first-person plural language such as “we.” Such sections also occur in Acts 16, 20–21, and 27–28, but what they reveal about the narrative’s sources or authorship remains disputed. Codex Bezae and related witnesses also preserve a notably distinctive form of Acts often called the Western text. These questions require case-by-case judgment: neither the voyage’s vivid narration nor a manuscript’s distinctive readings settle the historical or textual issues by themselves.
